svg.title: Tech abuse runs through four kinds of ordinary consumer feature
svg.desc: Four boxes listing the channels through which technology-facilitated abuse most often runs in intimate relationships, all of them features designed for families and partners. The first is account access and shared plans: passwords the other person already knows or can guess, a shared Apple ID or Google account, Apple Family Sharing and carrier family plans, Google Family Link, and password reset mail arriving at a shared number or mailbox. The second is location tracking: Find My and Google Maps location sharing, Bluetooth trackers such as AirTags, connected-car apps, shared calendars, and GPS coordinates carried by synced photos. The third is stalkerware installed while the other person briefly has your phone, which forwards messages, call logs, photos, browsing and location while showing no icon at all. The fourth is smart home and shared devices: smart locks, cameras, doorbells, thermostats, voice assistants and shared streaming accounts. The blue bar below notes that the most reliable signal is usually the other person knowing something they should not, and that the period around leaving is the most dangerous.
svg.text: What they share
Most of this needs no special skill. It
uses ordinary consumer features built
for families and partners, turned
against one person in the household.
Account access and shared plans
Passwords for your mailbox, phone
lock and banking that the other
person already knows or can guess
A shared Apple ID or Google account,
which syncs messages, photos, browsing
history and contacts to their device
Apple Family Sharing and carrier family
plans, exposing purchases and installed apps
Google Family Link, a parental tool that
becomes surveillance when pointed at an adult
Reset mail arriving at a shared number or mailbox,
so a new password does not lock them out
Location tracking
Find My and Google Maps location
sharing, which keeps running once
enabled and sends no further notice
Bluetooth trackers such as AirTags or Tile,
placed in a bag, a car or a child's belongings
Connected-car apps showing
live position and trip history
Shared calendars, which
reveal where you will be next
Photos synced with GPS coordinates
attached, enough to locate a new address
Stalkerware on the device
Installed while the other person briefly
has your phone, then forwarding messages,
call logs, photos, browsing and location
Able to show no icon at all
A battery that drains faster, a warm
phone at idle and unexplained data
use are all hints rather than proof
Smart home and shared devices
Smart locks, cameras, doorbells and
thermostats. Whoever holds the controlling
account sees the footage, knows when the
door opens and can lock you out
After separation these often
stay on the other account
A shared voice assistant
exposes routines and reminders
Shared streaming and location-based
social apps leak your daily pattern
The most reliable signal
Every hint above has other explanations. In
practice the most reliable signal is the other
person knowing something they should not.
